decks.title: Creative Writing — Part 1: Classified Advertisements and Posters
goals: Write a classified advertisement of up to 50 words in telegraphic style
Choose the right heading and the essential details for each category
Plan and write a poster with title, slogan, facts, organiser and contact
Describe visual appeal in a text-only answer

slides.heading: Creative Writing — Part 1: Advertisements and Posters
slides.body_md: In the school paper, creative writing carries **16 marks**: classified advertisement 3, poster 3, speech 5, debate 5, each with an internal choice. This part covers the two 50-word tasks; Part 2 covers the speech and the debate.

visual.alt: Table of the creative writing tasks in the Class 11 school paper: a classified advertisement and a poster of up to fifty words for three marks each, and a speech and a debate of one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words for five marks each, sixteen marks in all.
visual.caption: Class 11 has no board exam: this is the school annual examination pattern.

slides.narration: Welcome to creative writing. In the school paper this section carries sixteen marks. A classified advertisement and a poster are worth three marks each, in up to fifty words. A speech and a debate are worth five marks each, in one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words. Each has a choice. In this part we master the two short tasks.

slides.heading: What a classified advertisement is
slides.body_md: A short paid notice in a newspaper column, set under a **heading**. You may be asked for sale, to let, situation vacant, lost and found, or tuition notices.

headers: What the reader looks for first
rows: the item, its condition and the price
the post, qualifications, salary, how to apply
description, place and time, whom to call

visual.alt: Table of five classified columns with their heading and the details a reader looks for first: for sale, to let, situation vacant, lost and found, and tuition.
visual.caption: Matrimonial advertisements are not part of this syllabus task.

slides.narration: A classified advertisement is a short paid notice, placed in a newspaper column under a heading. The syllabus asks for notices such as for sale, to let, situation vacant, lost and found, and tuition. Each column has its own heading and its own reader, who looks for particular details first. Matrimonial advertisements are not part of this task, so do not use them.

slides.heading: Write like a classified: every word costs money
columns:
**Wordy (avoid)**

- full sentences and greetings
- *I would like to inform you that…*
- praise: *wonderful, very nice*
- long explanations of why you are selling

**Classified style (use)**

- short phrases, no greetings
- heading says the rest
- facts: size, age, condition, price
- contact line at the end

rows: I would like to inform you that I wish to sell
which is in a very good working condition
may kindly contact me on the following number
available at a price of rupees six thousand

visual.alt: Table that turns wordy phrases into classified style: delete the announcing sentence, shorten the condition, replace the request with the word Contact, and write the price as a figure.

slides.narration: Newspapers charge by the word, so every extra word costs the advertiser money. Drop the greetings and the announcing sentences, because the heading already says what the notice is. Replace praise with facts: size, age, condition, price. End with a contact line. The table shows four wordy phrases and their classified versions.

slides.heading: The parts of a classified advertisement
slides.body_md: Heading in capitals; then item or post; key details; price or terms; place; **Contact:** line. Abbreviations are fine only if readers know them, such as *2BHK*.

visual.alt: Flow of the six parts of a classified advertisement: heading, item or post, key details, price or terms, place, and contact line.
visual.caption: Read left to right; keep every part short.

slides.narration: Here are the parts of a classified advertisement. A heading in capitals. Then the item or the post. Then the key details. Then the price or terms, then the place, and last a contact line. You may use shorthand that every reader knows, like two B H K for a flat, but never invent your own abbreviations, because readers will have to guess.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: planning a Wanted advertisement
slides.body_md: *Task:* Mrs Kulkarni of Bhopal wants to buy a second-hand sewing machine, working, up to ₹4,000, and will collect it herself.
bullets: **Heading:** WANTED
**Item and condition:** second-hand sewing machine, in working order, hand or electric
**Terms:** budget up to ₹4,000; buyer collects
**Place:** anywhere in Bhopal
**Contact:** Mrs Kulkarni, with a number in the form 98XXXXXX10
slides.narration: Plan first. Choose the heading, here Wanted. Then list the item and its condition, the terms, the place, and the contact. This takes one minute. Notice that every line is a fact a seller needs. There is no greeting, and no sentence about why the machine is wanted, because that would cost words and help nobody.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the finished advertisement
slides.body_md:
**WANTED**  
Second-hand sewing machine, hand-operated or electric, in working order. Budget up to ₹4,000. Buyer will collect from anywhere in Bhopal.  
Contact: Mrs Kulkarni, 98XXXXXX10
slides.narration: Here is the finished advertisement. It has a heading, the item with its condition, the budget, the place, and the contact line. It is about thirty words, well inside the limit of fifty. Count the words yourself, including the heading, because the examiner does. If you have words to spare, add a useful fact, not decoration.

slides.heading: Check: shorthand readers understand
slides.narration: Time to check yourself. Which of these abbreviations would readers understand at once in a to let advertisement? Remember the rule about shorthand.

slides.heading: Categories and the details people forget
slides.body_md: Each category has one detail that is easy to forget. Run a quick checklist before you write the contact line.

headers: Detail that is easy to forget
rows: Graduate; experience preferred; salary; apply in person
brown, 8 months old, red collar; reward
where and when it was lost
owner may claim by describing the contents
one detail kept back for proof
small batches; weekly tests; free demo class

visual.alt: Table of four classified categories with typical short phrases and a detail that is easy to forget: last date for a vacancy, place and time for a lost item, a withheld detail for a found item, and the classes covered for a tuition advertisement.

slides.narration: Each category has a detail writers often forget. In a vacancy, the way to apply and the last date. In a lost notice, where and when the item was lost. In a found notice, keep one detail back, so that only the true owner can claim it. In a tuition notice, the classes and board covered. A quick checklist before the contact line saves marks.

slides.heading: Check: match the column to the details
slides.narration: Match each kind of advertisement with the details its reader needs most. Think about who is reading and what they would ask first.

slides.heading: What a poster must do
slides.body_md: A poster is read in seconds, so it gives **essential information** and has **visual appeal**. In the exam you show visual appeal in words: a bold title, short lines, and where a picture or border would go.

rows: tells a passer-by the subject at a glance
a catchy line that stays in the mind
Who may join, what to bring
builds trust and lets people ask
draws the eye; in the exam, say what you would draw

visual.alt: Table of the elements of a poster: bold title, slogan, date, time and venue, who may join, organiser and contact, and a picture or border for visual appeal.

slides.narration: A poster is read in a few seconds, by someone walking past. So it must give the essential information and it must catch the eye. Start with a bold title and a slogan. Then give date, time and venue, who may join, the organiser and a contact. In a text answer, show visual appeal with short lines, space, and a note on any picture or border.

slides.heading: Poster layout zones
slides.body_md: Think in zones from top to bottom, and keep the whole text within 50 words, counting every word including the title.

visual.caption: Poster layout zones, top to bottom.

slides.narration: Think of the poster in zones from top to bottom. The title is first and largest. The slogan sits below it. Then a picture or border, then a block with the date, time, venue and who may join. Last, a strip with the organiser and the contact. Plan the zones, then fill each with the fewest words, counting every word including the title.

slides.heading: Weak poster, strong poster
columns:
**Weak**

- *Come and enjoy!!! Fun for all!!!*
- one long paragraph
- no organiser or contact
- borrowed slogan

**Strong**

- exact dates, time, venue on separate lines
- short lines with space
- organiser named, one contact
- original slogan

rows: Come and enjoy!!! Fun for all!!!
Dates, time and venue, each on its own line
Short lines with space between them
An original slogan that fits the cause

visual.alt: Table that compares a weak poster with a strong one: a vague call against exact details, a paragraph against short lines, no organiser against a named organiser, and a borrowed slogan against an original one.

slides.narration: Compare a weak poster with a strong one. The weak one shouts with exclamation marks but gives no facts. The strong one gives the exact date, time and venue on separate short lines, names the organiser and gives one contact. Its slogan is original and suits the cause. Short lines and space also make it look better.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a tree plantation poster
slides.body_md: *Task:* The Green Brigade of Jubilee School will plant saplings on Sunday 21 July at 7 am at the Jubilee Park gate. Students and families may join.

headers: Content for the tree plantation poster
rows: PLANT A TREE, GROW A FUTURE
Dig a little, breathe a lot
Sunday, 21 July, 7 am; Jubilee Park gate
students and families; saplings and gloves provided

visual.alt: Table that plans a tree plantation poster by zone: title, slogan, facts, who may join and what is provided, and organiser and contact.

slides.narration: Plan by zones. The title is the message: plant a tree, grow a future. The slogan is a short original line. The facts are the day, date, time and the meeting point. Then who may join and what is provided, which removes doubts. Last, the organiser and a contact. Notice that the plan is a table of short lines, not sentences.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the finished poster
slides.body_md:
**PLANT A TREE, GROW A FUTURE**  
*Dig a little, breathe a lot*  
Sunday, 21 July, 7 am  
Meeting point: Jubilee Park gate  
Saplings and gloves provided. Students and families welcome.  
Organised by: Green Brigade, Jubilee School  
Contact: 98XXXXXX10
slides.narration: Here is the finished poster, written line by line. It has a title, a slogan, the date and time, the meeting point, who may join, the organiser and a contact. It is about forty words. If you are asked to show visual appeal, add a short note such as a border of leaves, but do not spend words on it.

slides.heading: Check: what a poster needs
slides.narration: Which of these is least necessary on a poster announcing a school music evening? Think about what a passer-by can read in a few seconds.

slides.heading: Check: the catchy line
slides.narration: Fill in the blank. A short, catchy line on a poster that is easy to remember is called what? Then check your answer.

slides.heading: How the 3-mark tasks are marked
slides.body_md: Half a mark for format and layout, one and a half for content, one for expression. Content is the biggest share.

rows: A suitable heading in capitals (FOR SALE, TO LET, SITUATION VACANT, LOST, FOUND, TUITION) and a contact line at the end; compact classified layout.
Every essential detail for the category (item or post, key features, price or terms, place, how to respond); nothing that contradicts the brief.
Telegraphic, economical wording with no wasted words; correct grammar and spelling; within 50 words.

visual.alt: Table of the SOYL rubric for a classified advertisement: format and layout half a mark, content one and a half marks, expression one mark.
visual.caption: SOYL rubric for 3-mark tasks; the same split is used for the poster.

slides.narration: Here is how a three mark task is usually marked. Half a mark for format and layout. One and a half marks for content: every essential detail present. One mark for expression: economical wording, correct grammar and the word limit. The poster uses the same split, with the slogan counted under expression.

slides.heading: Summary: advertisements and posters
bullets: Classified advertisement: heading, item, key details, price or terms, place, **Contact:** line.
Short phrases; every word costs money; no greetings.
Poster: bold title, slogan, date, time, venue, who may join, organiser, contact.
Both: up to 50 words, counting every word including the heading.

visual.alt: Flow of the six parts of a classified advertisement: heading, item or post, key details, price or terms, place, and contact line.
visual.caption: Read left to right; keep every part short.

slides.narration: To sum up. A classified advertisement has a heading, the item, key details, price or terms, place and a contact line, all in short phrases. A poster has a bold title, a slogan, the date, time and venue, who may join, the organiser and a contact. Both must stay within fifty words, counting every word, and both reward facts over decoration.

slides.heading: Exam tips: advertisements and posters
bullets: Plan for one minute; write the heading first.
Count words, including the heading and the contact line.
Use only the names and facts given; add small details only if the question allows.
Use the masked number form 98XXXXXX10 if a number is needed.
Common slips: greeting words, missing price or venue, invented abbreviations, a poster written as a paragraph.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Plan for a minute and write the heading first. Count the words, including the heading and the contact line. Use the facts given in the question, and add small details only when the question allows. Avoid greeting words, forgotten prices or venues, invented abbreviations, and a poster written as one long paragraph.

decks.title: Creative Writing — Part 2: Speech and Debate
goals: Write a speech of 120-150 words in the order salutation, opening, body, conclusion, thanks
Suit the tone, examples and requests to the audience
Write a debate speech for or against a motion with an address, stand, arguments and rebuttal
Answer an opposing argument fairly and persuasively

slides.heading: Creative Writing — Part 2: Speech and Debate
slides.body_md: Two **5-mark** tasks of **120-150 words**, each with a choice. Both are spoken pieces: write for the ear, with short sentences and a clear order.

visual.alt: Table of the creative writing tasks in the Class 11 school paper: a classified advertisement and a poster of up to fifty words for three marks each, and a speech and a debate of one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words for five marks each, sixteen marks in all.
visual.caption: Class 11 has no board exam: this is the school annual examination pattern.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two, the speech and the debate. Each is worth five marks, in one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words, and each comes with a choice. Both are meant to be spoken, so write for the ear: short sentences, a clear order, and a voice that sounds like a person talking to a room.

slides.heading: Who is listening? Occasion decides tone
slides.body_md: Before writing, name the **occasion**, the **audience** and the **tone**. The same topic needs a different speech for different listeners.

visual.alt: Table of speech occasions with the audience and tone: school assembly, farewell or welcome, parents' meeting, and debate.

slides.narration: Before you write, name the occasion, the audience and the tone. An assembly speech is lively and simple. A farewell is warm and thankful. A speech to parents is respectful and practical. A debate is firm but polite. The same topic needs a different speech for a different audience, and examiners reward the writer who notices.

slides.heading: The five parts of a speech
slides.body_md: Salutation → opening hook → body (two or three points, each with an example) → conclusion with a call to action → thanks.

nodes.label: Body: two or three points with examples

visual.alt: Flow of the five parts of a speech from top to bottom: salutation, opening hook, body with points and examples, conclusion with a call to action, and thanks.
visual.caption: Speech: 120-150 words.

slides.narration: A speech has five parts. First the salutation, greeting the audience in order of rank. Then an opening that hooks the listeners, such as a question or a short scene. Then the body, with two or three points, each with an example. Then a conclusion with a call to action. And last, thanks. Keep to this order and you will score the format mark.

slides.heading: Salutation and opening
columns:
**Salutation**

- *Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and dear friends.*
- most senior person first
- match the occasion: *Good evening, respected parents…*

**Opening hooks**

- a question to the audience
- a short, vivid scene
- a surprising fact you are sure of
- avoid *Today I will speak about…*

rows: persuade the House on a motion

visual.alt: Table that compares a speech with a debate: aim, address, parts, tone and length.

slides.narration: Begin with a salutation that names the most senior person first and suits the occasion. Then hook your listeners. A question, a short scene or a surprising fact you are sure of works well. Avoid the dull opening, today I will speak about, which wastes your best seconds. The table also shows how a speech differs from a debate.

slides.heading: Devices that help a listener
slides.body_md: A listener cannot re-read, so use devices that make points memorable. Use two or three, not ten.

rows: Who will plant the first tree?
We can learn, we can lead, we can change.

visual.alt: Table of four speech devices with a sample sentence and its effect: rhetorical question, repetition in threes, direct address, and contrast.

slides.narration: A listener cannot go back and re-read, so use devices that make a point easy to remember. A rhetorical question makes people think. Repeating a phrase three times gives rhythm. Direct address, such as friends, involves the audience. A contrast sharpens a point. Use two or three of these with care, because too many sound artificial.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: planning a speech on punctuality
slides.body_md: *Task:* Speak at the morning assembly on punctuality (120-150 words).

headers: Plan for a speech on punctuality
rows: Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and friends
a question: who has run the last hundred metres to the gate?
point 1: time is shared (a late student delays the class); point 2: habit builds character; example: a train that does not wait
set the alarm ten minutes early tomorrow

visual.alt: Table that plans a speech on punctuality: salutation, a question as the opening, two points with an example as the body, a call to set the alarm earlier as the conclusion, and thanks.

slides.narration: Here is the plan for a speech on punctuality. The opening is a question every student recognises. The body has two points and one example: time is shared, so a late student delays the class, and a habit of being on time builds character. The conclusion is one simple action, setting the alarm ten minutes early. Then thanks.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the finished speech
slides.body_md:
Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends.

Who here has run the last hundred metres to the gate this week? Be honest. Today I want to speak about a small habit with a big effect: being on time.

First, time is shared. When one student walks in late, the teacher pauses, the class turns and thirty minutes of learning shrink by a little. Second, punctuality is a habit that grows into character. The student who keeps appointments with the clock will keep promises to people. A train does not wait for anyone, and neither does opportunity.

So let us begin tomorrow. Set your alarm ten minutes earlier and arrive with time to spare.

Thank you.
slides.narration: Here is the finished speech, about one hundred and thirty words. Follow the order: salutation, a question that hooks, two points with the train as an example, a conclusion with one clear action, and thanks. Notice the short sentences and the friendly voice. It sounds like a student talking, not a textbook being read aloud.

slides.heading: Check: order the parts of a speech
slides.narration: Put the five parts of a speech in the order in which they are delivered. Start with the greeting and end with the thanks.

slides.heading: The debate speech
slides.body_md: A debate is about a **motion**. You speak **for** or **against** it, to the **chair**, the **judges** and the **House**, and you answer the other side.

nodes.label: Address the chair, judges and the House
State your stand on the motion

visual.alt: Flow of the six parts of a debate speech: address, stand, first argument, second argument, rebuttal, and conclusion with thanks.
visual.caption: Debate: 120-150 words.

slides.narration: A debate speech is built on a motion, a statement the House is asked to accept. You speak for it or against it. You address the chairperson, the judges, your opponents and the House. After your arguments you include a rebuttal, answering a point from the other side. You end by restating your stand and thanking the House.

slides.heading: Address, stand and tone
columns:
**Address**

- *Respected Chairperson, honourable judges, worthy opponents and friends.*
- chair first, then judges, then the other side
- end: *I urge the House to… Thank you.*

**Stand and tone**

- state your side in the first two sentences
- attack arguments, never people
- *With due respect…*, *My opponent has overlooked…*
- signpost: *First… Second… Finally…*

rows: persuade the House on a motion

visual.alt: Table that compares a speech with a debate: aim, address, parts, tone and length.

slides.narration: Open by addressing the chairperson first, then the judges, then your opponents and friends. State your side in the first two sentences, so that nobody has to guess it. Keep your tone firm but courteous. Attack arguments, never people. Phrases like with due respect and my opponent has overlooked keep the register formal, and signposting words keep the speech clear.

slides.heading: Rebuttal: answer the exact claim
slides.body_md: Accept what is fair, **answer the exact claim**, and support your reply with a reason or an example. Never attack the person.

rows: Character shows in conduct, not clothes
a student known for kindness, not for her shoes
One set lasts a year; fashion changes monthly
compare the cost of casual wear
Shared rules give everyone equal footing
no one is judged by brand

visual.alt: Table of three opposing claims about school uniforms with a reply and a support for each: individuality, cost, and freedom.
visual.caption: Pattern: accept what is fair, answer the exact claim, support the reply.

slides.narration: A rebuttal answers the point the other side actually made. First accept what is fair in it. Then give your reply, and support it with a reason or example. In the table, each claim about uniforms gets a reply and a support. Never change the subject, never agree with the other side, and never attack the person.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a debate speech
slides.body_md: *Task:* Speak **for** the motion "Uniforms should be compulsory in schools" (120-150 words).

headers: Plan: for the motion "Uniforms should be compulsory"
rows: chair, judges, opponents; in favour of the motion
equality: no one judged by clothes
time and money saved on daily choice
individuality: shown in conduct, not clothing

visual.alt: Table that plans a debate speech for school uniforms: address and stand, equality as the first argument, time and money as the second, a rebuttal on individuality, and a closing appeal.

slides.narration: Here is the plan for a debate speech in favour of compulsory uniforms. After the address and the stand, the first argument is equality: no one is judged by clothes. The second is time and money saved on the daily choice. Then a rebuttal of the claim that uniforms hide individuality, and a closing appeal with thanks.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the finished debate speech
slides.body_md:
Respected Chairperson, honourable judges, worthy opponents and friends.

I rise in favour of the motion that uniforms should be compulsory in schools.

First, a uniform makes every child equal. No one arrives worried that a classmate will judge their clothes. Second, it saves time and money: families do not argue every morning over what to wear, and one set lasts a year.

My opponents say uniforms hide individuality. But individuality lives in what we think, say and do. A student is remembered for her kindness or her curiosity, never for her shirt.

A school is a place to grow together, and a uniform reminds us that we do.

I urge the House to support the motion. Thank you.
slides.narration: Here is the finished debate speech. It begins with the address and states the stand at once. Two arguments follow, each with a reason. Then the rebuttal answers the exact claim about individuality. The closing lines restate the stand, appeal to the House and say thank you. It is about one hundred and thirty words.

slides.heading: Check: what a rebuttal is
slides.narration: In a debate speech, what is a rebuttal? Choose the answer that describes its job on the page.

slides.heading: Speech or debate: which is which
slides.body_md: Same length, different job. A speech welcomes, informs or inspires; a debate **persuades on a motion**.

rows: persuade the House on a motion

visual.alt: Table that compares a speech with a debate: aim, address, parts, tone and length.

slides.narration: Both tasks are written in one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words, but they do different jobs. A speech welcomes, informs or inspires an audience. A debate persuades the House on a motion. A speech has a hook, a body and a call to action. A debate has a stand, arguments, a rebuttal and an appeal.

slides.heading: Check: spot the device
slides.narration: Which device does this sentence use? Can we call a river clean when fish cannot live in it? Pick the best name.

slides.heading: Check: match the terms
slides.narration: Match each term with its meaning. Take your time over salutation, motion, rebuttal and slogan.

slides.heading: How speeches and debates are marked
slides.body_md: Five marks each: format 1, content 2, expression 2. Content needs developed points, not a list of slogans.

rows: Salutation, a hook in the opening, a body, a conclusion and thanks, in that order.
Relevant points, each developed with a fact, example or suggestion; suits the audience and the occasion.
Clear spoken style, rhetorical devices used with care, linking words, correct grammar; 120-150 words.

visual.alt: Table of the SOYL rubric for a speech: format one mark, content two marks, expression two marks.
visual.caption: SOYL rubric for 5-mark tasks; the debate uses the same split.

slides.narration: Here is how a five mark task is usually marked. One mark for format: salutation, opening, body, conclusion and thanks in order, or the debate address, stand and rebuttal. Two marks for content: developed points with support. Two marks for expression: clear spoken style, devices used with care, linking words, correct grammar and the word limit.

slides.heading: Summary: speech and debate
bullets: Speech: salutation → hook → body with examples → conclusion → thanks.
Match tone, examples and requests to the audience.
Debate: address → stand → arguments → rebuttal → appeal and thanks.
Rebuttal answers the exact claim; attack arguments, never people.
Both: 120-150 words; write for the ear.

nodes.label: Body: two or three points with examples

visual.alt: Flow of the five parts of a speech from top to bottom: salutation, opening hook, body with points and examples, conclusion with a call to action, and thanks.
visual.caption: Speech: 120-150 words.

slides.narration: To sum up. A speech runs salutation, hook, body with examples, conclusion and thanks. Match the tone and the examples to the audience. A debate runs address, stand, arguments, rebuttal and appeal. The rebuttal answers the exact claim, and you attack arguments, never people. Both are written for the ear, in one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty words.

notes.title: Creative Writing: Class 11 English Core notes

sections.heading: 1. Creative writing in the school paper
sections.body_md:
Creative writing carries **16 marks** in the Class 11 school annual examination: a **classified advertisement** (3) and a **poster** (3), each in up to **50 words**, and a **speech** (5) and a **debate** (5), each in **120-150 words**. Each has an internal choice in the school paper.

Plan for one or two minutes. Count words, including headings.

key_terms.definition_md: Two questions of the same marks from which the student answers one.
The maximum length: 50 words for advertisements and posters, 150 for speeches and debates.

sections.heading: 2. Classified advertisements: format and economy
sections.body_md:
A classified advertisement is a short paid notice in a column of a newspaper. Parts, in order: **heading** in capitals, item or post, key details, price or terms, place, **Contact:** line.

Newspapers charge by the word, so write in short phrases: no greetings, no announcing sentences, no praise. Use only shorthand readers know (*2BHK*). Write the contact in the masked form *98XXXXXX10* when a number is required.

key_terms.definition_md: A short paid notice set under a heading in a newspaper column.
Writing in short phrases that drop words the reader can supply.

sections.heading: 3. Categories of classified advertisement
sections.body_md:
**For sale:** item, condition, price. **To let:** size, locality, rent, facilities. **Situation vacant:** post, qualifications, salary, how to apply. **Lost / found:** description, place, time, whom to contact; for a found item, keep one detail back. **Tuition:** subjects, classes, quality, place.

Matrimonial advertisements are not used for this task.

sections.heading: 4. Posters
sections.body_md:
A poster is read in seconds, so it carries **essential information** and **visual appeal**: a bold title, a catchy **slogan**, date, time and venue, who may join, the organiser and a contact.

In a text answer, put each fact on its own short line, leave visual appeal to layout and a short note about a picture or border, and keep within **50 words**, counting the title.

An **event** poster stresses facts; an **awareness** poster adds short actions people can take.

sections.heading: 5. Speeches: structure and audience
sections.body_md:
A speech is written for the ear and has five parts: **salutation** (most senior person first), an **opening** that hooks the audience, a **body** of two or three points with examples, a **conclusion** with a call to action, and **thanks**. Length: 120-150 words.

The occasion and the audience decide the tone: lively for an assembly, warm for a farewell, respectful and practical for parents.

sections.heading: 6. Speeches: devices and style
sections.body_md: Listeners cannot re-read, so use a few devices that help memory: a **rhetorical question**, **repetition in threes**, **direct address** and **contrast**. Keep sentences short, link points with *First, Second, Finally*, and avoid slang and long words that sound artificial.

key_terms.definition_md: A question asked for effect, not for an answer.

sections.heading: 7. Debates and rebuttal
sections.body_md:
A debate is held on a **motion**. A speaker takes a side and addresses the **chairperson**, the **judges**, the opponents and **the House**. Order: address, **stand**, arguments with support, **rebuttal**, concluding appeal and thanks. Length: 120-150 words.

A rebuttal accepts what is fair, answers the exact claim and supports the reply. Attack arguments, never people.

key_terms.definition_md: The statement on which a debate is held.
A reply that answers and weakens a point made by the other side.

sections.heading: 8. How the tasks are marked
sections.body_md:
SOYL rubrics, modelled on the school paper: **advertisement and poster (3):** format and layout 0.5, content 1.5, expression 1. **Speech and debate (5):** format 1, content 2, expression 2.

Content has the largest share in every task; exceeding the word limit and missing essentials cost marks.

The language: economy, accuracy and style.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Marks:** creative writing 16 = classified advertisement 3 + poster 3 + speech 5 + debate 5 (school annual examination, Class 11), each with a choice.

**How marks are awarded:** advertisement and poster — format and layout 0.5, content 1.5, expression 1; speech and debate — format 1, content 2, expression 2 (SOYL rubric modelled on the school pattern).

**Common mistakes — advertisement and poster**
1. Greeting words and full sentences in a classified advertisement.
2. Missing price, venue, date or contact.
3. Invented abbreviations; going over 50 words.
4. A poster written as a paragraph instead of short lines.

**Common mistakes — speech and debate**
1. A casual greeting instead of a formal salutation.
2. No hook; a body that lists points without examples.
3. A debate with no clear stand, no rebuttal or a personal attack.
4. A new argument after the conclusion; no thanks.

**Time:** about 5 minutes for an advertisement or poster and 10 for a speech or debate, including planning and a word check.

A very good morning to our respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends.

How many of us finished a book last month? Please raise your hands. I see only a few. That is why I am speaking today about the joy of reading.

So here is a simple plan. Read twenty pages every night, borrow one book a week from our library, and share your favourite with a friend.

Let every bag in this school carry a book beside the lunch box. Thank you.

answer.model_answer_md:
Respected Chairperson, esteemed judges, worthy opponents and fellow students.

I rise to support the motion that mobile phones should be allowed in schools.

First, a phone is a dictionary, a calculator and a library in one pocket. A student who meets an unfamiliar word can look it up at once. Second, phones keep children safe. A parent can reach a child who is stranded after a late bus.

My opponents will say that phones distract. But distraction is a question of rules, not of devices. With phones kept in bags during lessons and used only with permission, we gain the benefits without the harm. We do not ban pencils because someone doodles.

Schools prepare us for the world, and in that world every citizen carries a phone. Let us teach responsible use instead of pretending the phone does not exist.

I urge the House to support the motion. Thank you.

The self-praise tells readers nothing they can act on, and the closing invitation can be shortened. The dates, venue, title and slogan are the content a poster exists to give.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: Which phrase is out of place in a formal debate speech?

options.text_md: With due respect to the other side
My worthy opponent has overlooked one fact

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** You people are talking nonsense. A debater attacks arguments, never people. Courteous phrasing keeps the register formal and the audience on the speaker's side.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.stem_md: A speaker ends: "Thank you, friends. Before I sit down, I must tell you that fast food causes heart disease, and that is why our canteen must change." What is the main flaw in this ending?

options.text_md: It uses the words thank you
It brings in a fresh argument after the thanks, so the speech has no real closing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It brings in a fresh argument after the thanks, so the speech has no real closing. A conclusion pulls the speech together and the thanks come last. A new argument after the thanks is unsupported and leaves the audience with a loose end.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

questions.stem_md: Motion: "School should start at 9 am instead of 8 am." Four arguments are offered for the motion. Which is the strongest?

options.text_md: Some of us like to sleep late on weekdays.
Adolescents need roughly eight to ten hours of sleep, and a later start lets those who study late come closer to it.
A school in another city is said to do it.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Adolescents need roughly eight to ten hours of sleep, and a later start lets those who study late come closer to it. The strongest argument is relevant to the aim of schooling, rests on a general fact and links the fact to the proposal. The others are personal preference, an unnamed example or a minor discomfort.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

questions.stem_md: A classified advertisement is normally written in full, flowing paragraphs.
questions.solution_md: **False.** It is written in short phrases, because every word costs money and space is limited.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (False)

questions.stem_md: In a debate, a speaker may call an opponent foolish when the opponent's argument seems very weak.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A debater may attack the argument but never the person; calling someone foolish loses the audience and the marks for tone.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (False)

questions.stem_md: A speech should not introduce a brand-new argument in its conclusion.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The conclusion gathers what has been said and ends with a call to action and thanks; a new argument there would be undeveloped.

marking_scheme.step: Correct choice (True)

questions.stem_md: A poster reads only: "ANNUAL DAY! Come and enjoy! Fun for all! Organised by Class 10." Name **two** essential items it lacks and say why each matters (30–50 words).
questions.solution_md: The essentials are what, when and where, plus a way to enquire. Naming any two missing items with the reason each matters earns the marks.

answer.model_answer_md: It lacks the date and time, so readers do not know when to attend. It also has no venue, so they cannot find the place. Contact details or entry information would help as well. The poster raises interest, but without these facts it cannot bring anyone to the event.

Reason given for each

questions.stem_md: Write a strong **opening sentence**, including the address to the audience (not more than 30 words), for a speaker **against** the motion "Social media does more good than harm."

questions.stem_md: Give **two** reasons why classified advertisements are written in short phrases rather than full sentences (30–50 words).
questions.solution_md: The two reasons are cost and space; ease of scanning is a related benefit for the reader.

answer.model_answer_md: Newspapers charge by the word or the line, so every extra word costs the advertiser money. Space on a page is also limited, and readers scan many advertisements quickly, so short phrases carrying key facts are easier to take in than long sentences.

marking_scheme.step: Reason 1 (cost per word)
Reason 2 (limited space or quick reading)

questions.stem_md: Motion: "Examinations should be replaced by projects." A speaker against the motion says, "Projects can be copied from the internet, so they cannot test real ability." Write a **two-sentence rebuttal** for the motion (30–50 words).
questions.solution_md: A good rebuttal accepts what is true in the claim, then shows with a practical fix why the conclusion does not follow.

answer.model_answer_md: My opponent is right that careless projects can be copied, but that is a fault of design, not of projects. Viva questions, drafts shown in class and tasks on local topics make copying difficult and test real understanding.

marking_scheme.step: Acknowledges and answers the exact claim
Gives a workable counter-point

questions.stem_md: A speech on water conservation ends: "That is all I wanted to say. Bye." Rewrite the ending in 30–50 words with a call to action and thanks.
questions.solution_md: A strong ending names one clear action, gives a reason that looks to the future and finishes with thanks, in a spoken style.

answer.model_answer_md: Friends, water is not ours to waste. Tomorrow, mend one leaking tap in your home and persuade one neighbour to do the same. Together, our small acts will keep our wells full for the next generation. Thank you for listening patiently.

marking_scheme.step: A specific call to action
A closing thought and thanks in a suitable register

questions.stem_md: Two posters for a school book fair. **P:** "BOOK FAIR / Come and buy books / At school / Best fair ever!!!" **Q:** "READ. SWAP. DISCOVER / Greenfield School Book Fair / 12 to 14 March, 9 am to 4 pm, School Library Hall / Second-hand book exchange; author talk on 13 March / Entry free". Which is better? Give three reasons (50–80 words).
questions.solution_md: Judge both against the essentials of a poster (facts, appeal, slogan) and decide with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Poster Q is better. First, it gives complete facts: dates, time, venue and free entry, whereas P does not say when or where. Second, it offers reasons to come, an exchange and an author talk. Third, its three-word slogan is catchy and sets the mood, while P relies on exclamation marks and a boast.

marking_scheme.step: Correct verdict (Q)
Reason 1 with evidence
Reasons 2 and 3 with evidence

questions.stem_md: Write the **body paragraph** of a speech for Class 9 students on the topic "Be kind online" (50–80 words). Give two points and one example.
questions.solution_md: A body paragraph in a speech states its points clearly, links them with signposting words and supports at least one with a short example.

answer.model_answer_md: Words typed on a screen hurt as much as words spoken in a corridor, and they travel further. First, think before you post: ask whether you would say it to the person's face. Second, stand up for a classmate who is mocked; a single kind comment can turn a lonely day around. Last year, one friendly message was enough to bring a withdrawn boy back into the group chat.

marking_scheme.step: Two clear points
A relevant example
Spoken style and signposting

questions.stem_md: Explain how a debate speech differs from an ordinary speech in its structure and in whom it addresses (50–80 words).
questions.solution_md: The differences are the fixed stand on a motion, the layered address, the rebuttal and the closing restatement.

answer.model_answer_md: A debate speech takes a firm stand on a stated motion and addresses the chairperson, the judges and the opponents. Besides its arguments it includes a rebuttal that answers the other side. It ends by restating the stand. An ordinary speech informs or inspires its audience without opposing anyone, so it needs no rebuttal.

marking_scheme.step: Stand on a motion and layered address
Rebuttal included
Contrast with an ordinary speech

questions.stem_md: Motion: "Every student should learn a musical instrument." The opposing speaker says, "Students already have too much to study; a new activity is only a burden." Write a **rebuttal paragraph** for the motion (50–80 words) with the claim, a counter-point and an example.
questions.solution_md: Take the claim of burden seriously, turn it with a reason (music as relief and discipline) and support it with a concrete example.

answer.model_answer_md: My opponent speaks of burden, but music is not a burden; it is relief. A student who practises the flute for twenty minutes returns to algebra calmer and more focused. Learning an instrument also teaches patience and regular practice, habits that help every subject. A busy timetable needs a balancing activity, and music is one that rewards effort quickly.

marking_scheme.step: Addresses the claim of burden directly
A reasoned counter-point
A concrete example

questions.stem_md: A student opens a speech to classmates with: "Hey guys, we all know exams are stressful, right?" Rewrite the opening for the **parents** at an annual function, and say in one sentence what you changed and why (50–80 words).
questions.solution_md: Adapting for a new audience changes the salutation, the register and the shared experience used for the hook.

answer.model_answer_md: Respected parents, teachers and guests, good evening. Many of you have sat beside a tired child at midnight, and you know how heavy examination season can feel. I changed the casual greeting into a formal salutation and spoke from the parents' own experience, because adults expect respect and respond to what they have lived.

marking_scheme.step: Formal salutation for the new audience
A hook drawn from the parents' experience
Explains the change
